verdict.narrative_for_user:
# Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_001

## What you've done well
Your evidence classification is genuinely careful. a_004 and a_010 both correctly mark the 1850/1860 household-position link as indirect evidence rather than overreaching -- you note explicitly that the relationship column wasn't added to the census until 1880, so co-residence isn't allowed to masquerade as a stated relationship. That's exactly the discipline Standards 38-39 ask for. And the tier itself is honestly calibrated: 'Probable,' not 'Proved,' with hedging language ('consistent with,' 'support a parent-child relationship') that actually matches the tier you chose -- no inflated claims riding on Probable-strength evidence.

## What to address before moving on
Two things stand between this and a defensible proof.

**This proof was finalized mid-research.** Look at what the project itself shows: q_001 is still `status: "in_progress"` -- it was never taken to `exhaustive_declared`, and `resolved`/`resolution_assertion_ids` are still empty. The plan (pl_002) has pli_006 -- the probate search for Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill Co. 1870-1890, which your own plan rationale flags as the item most likely to 'name Patrick as son' directly -- sitting at `status: "in_progress"` with zero log entries against it. The 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses were never attempted at all. Your own exhaustive_search_summary says as much. A will that could settle this outright hasn't even been searched yet; this proof shouldn't be called finished until it has (Standard 14/17, GPS Component 1).

**The death certificate informant is being trusted selectively.** James Brown supplied two facts on that 1908 certificate: Patrick's birthplace and Patrick's father. You reject his birthplace report as an error (Conflict Resolution section) but accept his father-name report as one of your three pillars of evidence -- without saying why the same secondary, absent-from-the-event informant is wrong about one fact and right about the other. That asymmetry is the first thing a peer reviewer will point to. It may well be defensible (family lineage is often better-preserved knowledge than exact birthplace), but the narrative needs to say so rather than leave it silent (Standard 43).

## Worth considering
- The Evidence Summary calls the three supporting facts 'independent lines of evidence,' but two of them (1850 and 1860 co-residence) likely trace back to the same recurring household informant across both censuses -- your own c_001 independence_analysis raises this exact doubt for the birthplace fact, but it doesn't carry through to how you characterize the parentage evidence. Consider softening the framing.
- Neither hypotheses[] nor conflicts[] addresses whether 'Thomas Flynn' could be more than one man in Schuylkill County across this period -- a real question given how common Irish surnames were in that mining county at the time. Your age-progression argument (5 to 15) helps, but a quick check for other same-named households would close this gap outright.
- Small housekeeping: a_002, the 1850 birthplace assertion your Conflict Resolution section leans on, is tagged to q_002 rather than q_001 -- worth retagging for a cleaner audit trail.

## What would change my mind
On the first point: an executed probate search (even a documented nil result) plus attempts at the 1870/1880/1900 census, followed by a fresh conclusion-readiness pass, would close the exhaustiveness gap outright.

On the second: a sentence in the Conflict Resolution or Assessment section explaining why Brown's paternity report deserves more trust than his birthplace report -- or, absent that, dialing back how much weight a_013 carries toward 'Probable' -- resolves the asymmetry.

| 5 *(fallback 4)* | Probate/estate | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1870–1910 | Ancestry | If FamilySearch probate is incomplete |
| 6 | Cemetery records | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1870–1910 | Find A Grave / USGenWeb | Headstone inscription = death date before civil registration |
| 7 | Newspaper obituaries | Muhlenberg Co., KY, 1870–1910 | Newspapers.com / KY Digital | Death notice may give date and place directly |
| 8 *(FAN)* | Children's death certs | KY statewide, 1911–1960 | Ancestry | A child's certificate listing Elijah as parent may record his death date |

Elijah was alive through at least 1870, so this window does not cover his death — but checking it confirms he is not in this register and rules out a data-entry anomaly in the birth year. FamilySearch 'Kentucky Death Records, 1852-1910' includes this early series.

The 1880 Federal Census is the first post-1870 enumeration. Finding Elijah alive in 1880 narrows the death window to 1880–1910 and may provide household context (wife, children) useful for probate and obituary searches. His absence confirms death before June 1880. FamilySearch indexes the 1880 census fully and freely.

A will or estate administration file for Elijah Wilkins in Muhlenberg County Circuit or County Court would record his death indirectly — the filing date sets a terminus post quem, heirs named corroborate family relationships, and the inventory may place him at a specific locality. Muhlenberg County estate records are partially digitized on FamilySearch. Date range runs from last known living date to the outer bound of plausible survival; lifespan of a man born c. 1814 sets the upper bound around 1900.

Fallback for FamilySearch probate search (pli_004). Ancestry holds Kentucky county court records for some jurisdictions not yet on FamilySearch, including portions of Muhlenberg County deed and probate microfilm. If FamilySearch yields nothing, Ancestry's 'Kentucky, Wills and Probate Records, 1774-1989' is the next check.

Cemetery inscriptions often supply death dates for individuals who died before civil registration. Find A Grave and BillionGraves index many Muhlenberg County cemeteries. A headstone for Elijah Wilkins with a death date would be derivative evidence corroborating the certificate search, or primary when no certificate exists. Also check the Kentucky Cemetery Records project (USGenWeb) for Muhlenberg County transcriptions.

Local newspapers occasionally published death notices and obituaries for long-time residents. The Greenville (Muhlenberg County seat) area press is partially digitized through Newspapers.com and the Kentucky Digital Newspaper Program. A death notice would supply the date and place directly and may name survivors useful for corroborating family context. This is a FAN-adjacent item: neighbors and associates named in an obituary can seed follow-on searches.

FAN item: death certificates of Elijah's children or spouse would name him as a parent or report his death date if the informant knew it. Children born c. 1840s–1860s could die 1911–1960, placing their certificates in the Kentucky mandatory-registration era. A child's certificate listing Elijah as father with his death date / birthplace would be secondary information about Elijah but directly relevant to the question. Search Ancestry's 'Kentucky Death Certificates, 1911-1965' for likely Wilkins surnames in Muhlenberg County.
